Here are the coolest seven games that you can play on your Apple Watch Series 10.

First up, Zombie Overkill. In this shooting game, you are facing off against a horde of zombies in the street. Shoot to kill, defeat all zombies and progress to the next level. You can get more members on your squad and unlock new weapons. The game gets more and more challenging as you move ahead in the game. If you like shooting games, then give it a try.

Next up is Tap to Dash. In this Flappy Bird inspired game, you tap on the screen to dash forward, passing through the open spaces, avoiding the pipes. Quickly pass the obstacle to increase the multiplier, and once it reaches five, you get a dash boost. It's frustratingly fun and super addictive. The kind of game that keeps you saying, "Just one more try."

Another similar game is Happy Rise. In this one, you have to constantly tap on the screen to keep the bird from falling. You have to go through different obstacles to move ahead and it's much harder than it looks. Apart from the first one, all the other obstacles shuffle around every time you hit the retry. It's a fun but challenging game, and I dare you to score just five points on this game. My high score is six.

Next up, Hit the Island. It was the first game specifically designed for interacting with the Dynamic Island. Now, it's also available on the Apple Watch. You have to hit the dynamic island at the top to score points and also save the ball from dropping. You can control the bottom bar via touch or using the scroll wheel. The speed of the ball increases as the game progresses. It's a really fun game.

In this 3D game, you play as Dare the Monkey. The aim in the game is to collect as many banana coins as you can while avoiding all the obstacles in the way, like wooden spikes, big birds, crates, etc. You can control the jump of the monkey through both the touch screen and the crown button. The all-time high score is displayed at the bottom. Mine is 40. Try to beat it.

Last but not the least, Snake Watch. The classic snake game on Apple Watch. In it, you have to eat as much as you can to grow as large as you can. But beware, if you try to eat any other snake, it's game over. Instead, you can trap them and if they try to eat you, they'll become your food.

question: Describe the audio content in detail.
answer:
A historical and biological overview of the thylacine, also known as the Tasmanian tiger. The narration explains that despite its wolf-like appearance, it was the largest carnivorous marsupial, known for its unique wide-opening jaw. It details the causes of its extinction, including hunting by European settlers, bounties, disease, and habitat loss. The audio concludes with the story of the last known thylacine, which died in a zoo in 1936, solidifying its status as a symbol of extinction and a warning about wildlife protection.

Speech content:
Once upon a time, in the wild landscapes of Tasmania, lived the thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger for the dark stripes across its back. Despite its wolf-like face, the thylacine was actually a marsupial, carrying its young in a pouch, just like kangaroos. It was the largest carnivorous marsupial of modern times, a shy and nocturnal hunter that fed on small animals and birds. Unlike dogs or wolves, its jaw could open to an astonishing 80 degrees, giving it a fearsome bite. Sadly, European settlers saw the thylacine as a threat to sheep and livestock. By the late 1800s, there were even government bounties that encouraged hunting. Disease, habitat loss, and competition with dogs only made things worse. The last known thylacine lived in Beaumaris Zoo in Hobart. Filmed in 1933 by naturalist David Fleay, it died just three years later, in 1936. That moment marked the end of a species that had survived for thousands of years. Today, the thylacine remains a powerful symbol of extinction and a reminder of the importance of protecting endangered wildlife before it's too late.

What announcement led to the Berlin Wall's collapse?
Imagine waking up one morning and hearing that the border you have been told is closed forever is suddenly open. That's exactly what happened on November 9, 1989, in East Berlin. A government official named Ginter Shabowski held a press conference and announced new travel rules. He said East Germans could now apply for permission to travel abroad without the strict restrictions they had known for decades. But here's the catch. He said the border would be opened immediately or without delay. No one expected such a quick change. People listening to the news thought it meant they could cross the border right away. Thousands of East Berliners flooded to the Berlin Wall, eager to see what was happening. Border guards, overwhelmed and unsure of what to do, eventually opened the gates. This spontaneous movement turned into a mass crossing, and the Berlin Wall, which had divided the city for nearly 30 years, was no longer a barrier. This announcement was part of broader reforms happening across the communist world. East Germany was feeling pressure from internal protests and from the Soviet Union, led by Mikhail Gorbachev, who was pushing for more openness and change. The East German government wanted to ease travel restrictions to calm unrest, but the public misunderstood the scope of the reforms. They believed the border was open for good, which was not exactly the plan. The fall of the Berlin Wall symbolized the weakening of communist control in East Germany and the entire Eastern Bloc. It showed that the socialist governments could no longer hold onto their strict borders or suppress demands for freedom. This event was a turning point that led to German reunification less than a year later, in October 1990. It also marked the beginning of the end for communist rule across Eastern Europe, as many countries experienced their own peaceful protests and reforms. So, the key moment was Ginter Shabowski's announcement during that press conference. It was a simple statement, but it sparked a chain reaction that changed history forever. It was the moment when the people's desire for freedom broke down the physical and political barriers that had divided Europe for so long.

answer:
A short audio clip with background music narrates a fascinating anecdote from April 1976, detailing the time Saturday Night Live producer Lorne Michaels made a live, on-air offer of $3,000 for The Beatles to reunite. The story highlights the incredible coincidence that John Lennon and Paul McCartney were watching the show together nearby and briefly considered accepting the offer. It also includes the follow-up skit where George Harrison humorously tried to claim the money, resulting in a classic SNL moment. This 'what if' scenario has become a legendary tale among music fans.

The speech content is as follows:
"In April 1976, six years after the Beatles' official breakup, an unusual moment in television history nearly triggered a legendary reunion. Lorne Michaels, the newly appointed producer of Saturday Night Live, made a bold and humorous pitch during a live broadcast. Looking straight into the camera, he offered the Beatles $3,000 to reunite on the SNL stage and perform three of their classic songs. Holding up a check, Michaels jokingly added that the money could be split however they wished, even suggesting that if they felt Ringo Starr didn't deserve an equal share, they were free to divide the funds accordingly. The proposal was clearly meant as satire, but fatefully, two of the Beatles, John Lennon and Paul McCartney, were watching the show that very night. McCartney happened to be visiting Lennon at his Dakota apartment in New York City, only a short cab ride away from the NBC studio. According to various sources, including Tom Doyle's Man on the Run, the two icons laughed heartily at Michaels' stunt. Lennon, amused, turned to McCartney and suggested, half-jokingly, 'Should we go down there and just do it?' They were reportedly close to calling a cab, but ultimately decided against it, citing the late hour and their desire to relax. It was a near-miss that fans have since romanticized as the Beatles reunion that almost happened. Although Lennon and McCartney didn't follow through, the moment lived on as a curious 'what if' in pop culture. Later that year, George Harrison appeared on SNL's cold open. In a scripted bit, he confronted Lorne Michaels to claim the $3,000. Michaels explained deadpan that the offer was intended for all four members and that Harrison alone was only entitled to $750. Harrison, staying in character, haggled for an extra $250 if he agreed to say the famous line, 'Live from New York, it's Saturday Night!' This whimsical series of events has become a cherished anecdote among Beatles fans, capturing a moment when a spontaneous, lighthearted invitation nearly brought together two of the world's most influential musicians. It stands as a testament to the Beatles' enduring presence in the public imagination and how even the most casual of gestures can ripple through music history."

question: Transcribe the speech content and output the transcription.
answer: From the 12th of October 2025, the EU will introduce new border checks known as the entry exit system, EES. As a part of its plans to strengthen border security, this is a new digital border system that will change requirements for British and other non-EU citizens traveling to the Schengen area, which encompasses all EU countries except for Cyprus and Ireland. It will also include the non-EU states, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, and Liechtenstein. The entry exit system is an automated IT system designed to register non-EU nationals traveling for short stays of up to 90 days in every 180 days. It will be used every time an individual crosses the external borders of any of the following countries. When EES is introduced, you may need to create a digital record on your first visit to the Schengen area at the port or airport on arrival. This will involve submitting your fingerprints, having your photo taken, and your passport scanned at dedicated booths. This new system will be introduced in phases over the first six months, and will eventually replace the current system of manually stamping passports when visitors arrive in the EU. You will not need to provide any information before traveling. At the port of Dover, Eurotunnel and Folkestone and Eurostar from St. Pancras, EES will be carried out before departure, as is currently the case for border checks. EES may take a few extra minutes to complete, so be prepared to wait during busy times at the border once the system starts. You can check with your travel operator to find out whether EES will affect your journey. Once registered, your digital record will be valid for three years. If you enter the Schengen area again during this time, you will only need to provide one biometric, either a photo or a fingerprint, at the border when you enter or exit. For more information, visit gov.uk/entry-exit system.

answer: Now deadly flooding in Indonesia has triggered sweeping government action against companies who are accused of worsening the disaster through deforestation. Permits have been revoked, lawsuits filed, and state takeovers threatened. But environmentalists warn the response may fall short and could even put fragile ecosystems at greater risk. After last year's catastrophic floods and landslides in Sumatra that killed more than a thousand people, officials under President Prabowo Subianto acknowledged that deforestation and overdevelopment played a major role in amplifying the disaster. Years of mining, plantation expansion, and forest fires have stripped vast stretches of rainforest across Sumatra, removing trees that once absorbed heavy rainfall and stabilized soil on steep hillsides. Dozens of companies have had their permits revoked, and the government plans to hand management of roughly 1 million hectares of land to a state enterprise. Initially, authorities indicated that the move would include the Martabe gold mine in the ecologically sensitive Batang Toru region, and conservationists have long accused the site of environmental damage. Officials now say that they are still reviewing possible violations, but critics note there's no indication development will halt in Batang Toru. Now, Batang Toru is home to the world's rarest great ape, the Tapanuli orangutan. Fewer than 800 were believed to exist in the wild before the floods. Using satellite data, experts estimate nearly 60 orangutans may have died in what they described as an extinction-level event for the species. Now, between 2001 and 2004, Sumatra lost 4.4 million hectares of forest. That's an area larger than Switzerland, making its landscapes increasingly vulnerable to landslides and flash flooding. Environmental groups warn that transferring land to state control does not guarantee better environmental practices. They say the government has yet to outline clear plans for forest recovery or long-term remediation. Now, lawsuits are seeking nearly $300 million from six companies, some funds earmarked for environmental repair. Experts argue far greater investment will be needed, and more firms may share responsibility.

question: Transcribe the speech content and output the transcription.
answer: Once upon a time, in the wild landscapes of Tasmania, lived the thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger for the dark stripes across its back. Despite its wolf-like face, the thylacine was actually a marsupial, carrying its young in a pouch, just like kangaroos. It was the largest carnivorous marsupial of modern times, a shy and nocturnal hunter that fed on small animals and birds. Unlike dogs or wolves, its jaw could open to an astonishing 80 degrees, giving it a fearsome bite. Sadly, European settlers saw the thylacine as a threat to sheep and livestock. By the late 1800s, there were even government bounties that encouraged hunting. Disease, habitat loss, and competition with dogs only made things worse. The last known thylacine lived in Beaumaris Zoo in Hobart. Filmed in 1933 by naturalist David Fleay, it died just three years later, in 1936. That moment marked the end of a species that had survived for thousands of years. Today, the thylacine remains a powerful symbol of extinction and a reminder of the importance of protecting endangered wildlife before it's too late.
